items.title: Jimmy Heath interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, September 8, 2014
items.q: [INTERVIEWER] ...remembering some of the things that Coltrane and Ornette Coleman did in the 60s... [INTERVIEWEE] Well I played “Ascension” once.

ctx.x: Well the way I look at improvisation, you know you can step out of the basic chord pattern if you make the connections. In other words, life is about connections. Everything musically is about connections. Socially it’s about connections. Connections is one of the biggest words in the English language. You’ve got to make a connection. And that’s what I’m talking about. If you see, like I remember Theodore “Fats” Navarro. Great trumpeter. And Fats used to play — if a woman walked in with a red dress on [scats]…

Oh, that’s terrific. Sometimes when I think about the history of jazz it has moved so fast it seems like. And I was remembering some of the things that Coltrane and Ornette Coleman did in the 60s. And now that seems like, wow, what is that, 50 years ago. I wonder what your reaction was to records like “Ascension” and free jazz.
Well I played “Ascension” once. © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-

items.title: Jimmy Heath — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I can’t think of his name now... Then, the Japanese had just given Ornette Coleman $150,000... I went to one other thing where Ornette got Carnegie or something? Me and George Wein were sitting together and they gave him $200,00 or something, for another award.

ctx.x: I guess one thing we should touch on is, we are here over the next few days celebrating the NEA Jazz Masters, and this 2010 crop of Jazz Masters. You were named an NEA Jazz Master in 2003, so you have been part of this group for some years now, and you have attended some of these events celebrating the Jazz Masters. Can you describe the experience of having that title given to you and being part of that group?

I love the title, “NEA Jazz Master”, and I appreciate what Dana Gioia, the gentleman who just retired, tried to do to give us more visibility and some kind of an equal exposure of other types of music. The other thing is, I found it ludicrous that they call my hero Dizzy Gillespie, a Jazz Master, and would give him $20,000 life achievement when some people are getting a MacArthur Award for $300,00 genius award like Max Roach, or somebody like Ornette Coleman, or somebody like the soprano player that lived in…
